courses.title: Critical Care and Perioperative Nursing
courses.description: Nursing care in intensive care and emergency settings, monitoring and life support, perioperative nursing across the surgical journey, and infection prevention in critical areas.

topics.title: Principles of Critical Care Nursing
topics.summary: Assessment of the critically ill, early warning scores, monitoring and family-centred care.

material.heading: Assessment and monitoring
material.body: Critical care nurses provide continuous assessment and intervention for patients with life-threatening conditions. The ABCDE approach structures assessment: Airway (patency, sounds), Breathing (rate, effort, SpO2, chest movement), Circulation (heart rate, blood pressure, capillary refill, urine output ≥ 0.5 mL/kg/h), Disability (GCS or AVPU, pupils, glucose) and Exposure (temperature, skin, wounds, drains). Early warning scores (e.g. NEWS2 — respiratory rate, SpO2, supplemental oxygen, temperature, systolic BP, heart rate, consciousness) trigger escalation; respiratory rate is the most sensitive early sign of deterioration. Monitoring: continuous ECG, invasive arterial pressure and central venous pressure (level the transducer at the phlebostatic axis — 4th intercostal space, mid-axillary line), pulse oximetry, capnography, fluid balance charts and blood gases. Nurse-to-patient ratio in ICU is ideally 1:1 for ventilated patients — often not achieved in Nigerian hospitals.

material.heading: Holistic and family care
material.body: Critically ill patients need pressure area care (turning every 2 hours, pressure-relieving mattresses, Braden scale risk assessment), eye care in sedated patients (lubricants, lid closure — prevent corneal exposure keratopathy), mouth care (chlorhexidine and toothbrushing reduce ventilator-associated pneumonia), nutrition (early enteral feeding), glycaemic control, bowel care, VTE prophylaxis, early mobilisation and sleep promotion. Delirium is common (screen with CAM-ICU) — reduce with minimal sedation, reorientation, sleep hygiene and family presence. Pain assessment in non-verbal patients uses behavioural scales (e.g. Behavioural Pain Scale, CPOT). Family-centred care: clear communication, involvement in decisions, flexible visiting, and psychological support; in Nigeria, the family often supports care and financing. End-of-life care in ICU requires compassionate communication, respect for cultural and religious practices, and comfort-focused care.

topics.title: Airway, Ventilation and Oxygen Therapy
topics.summary: Oxygen delivery devices, care of artificial airways, mechanical ventilation and suctioning.

material.heading: Oxygen therapy
material.body: Oxygen is a drug prescribed to target saturations: 94–98% for most patients; 88–92% for those at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure (COPD, obesity hypoventilation, neuromuscular disease). Delivery devices: nasal cannula (1–4 L/min — FiO2 about 24–40%), simple face mask (5–10 L/min — 40–60%; do not use below 5 L/min to avoid CO2 rebreathing), Venturi mask (fixed, accurate FiO2 24–60% — ideal in COPD), non-rebreather mask with reservoir bag (10–15 L/min — up to 85–90%; for emergencies), and high-flow nasal oxygen. Oxygen concentrators and cylinders are essential in Nigerian hospitals; oxygen shortages (highlighted during COVID-19) cost lives — pulse oximetry guides appropriate use. Humidify high-flow oxygen. Oxygen supports combustion — no smoking or naked flames.

material.heading: Artificial airways and ventilation
material.body: Endotracheal tubes and tracheostomies require: securing the tube (record tube position at the lips), cuff pressure 20–30 cmH2O (prevents aspiration and tracheal ischaemia), humidification, and suctioning when indicated (not routinely) — pre-oxygenate, use sterile technique, suction catheter no more than half the tube's internal diameter, apply suction on withdrawal only, limit to 10–15 seconds, and monitor SpO2 and heart rate (bradycardia from vagal stimulation). Ventilator care bundle to prevent VAP: head of bed 30–45°, daily sedation holds and spontaneous breathing trials, oral care, subglottic suction where available, and DVT and stress ulcer prophylaxis. Nurses monitor ventilator settings (mode, FiO2, PEEP, tidal volume, respiratory rate), alarms (high pressure — secretions, biting, bronchospasm; low pressure — disconnection or cuff leak), and patient–ventilator synchrony. Tracheostomy emergencies: blocked or displaced tube — keep spare tubes and obturator at the bedside.

topics.title: Emergency Nursing and Shock
topics.summary: Triage, resuscitation, shock recognition, fluid management and blood transfusion.

material.heading: Triage and resuscitation
material.body: Emergency department triage prioritises patients by acuity (e.g. South African Triage Scale — used in some Nigerian hospitals: red — emergency, orange — very urgent, yellow — urgent, green — routine, blue — dead). Nurses initiate resuscitation: basic life support (CPR 30:2 at 100–120 compressions/min, 5–6 cm depth, minimal interruptions, early defibrillation), assist with advanced life support, manage the airway, establish IV access (two large-bore cannulas), collect bloods, and document. Mass casualty incidents (road crashes, building collapses, explosions, insurgency) require triage using simple systems (START — walking wounded, respirations, perfusion, mental status) and hospital major incident plans. Trauma nursing follows <C>ABCDE with spinal precautions, haemorrhage control (direct pressure, tourniquets), and prevention of hypothermia.

material.heading: Shock and transfusion
material.body: Shock (inadequate tissue perfusion) presents with tachycardia, hypotension (late sign), cool clammy skin (warm in early septic shock), prolonged capillary refill, reduced urine output, confusion and raised lactate. Types: hypovolaemic (haemorrhage, dehydration, burns), cardiogenic, obstructive and distributive (septic, anaphylactic, neurogenic). Nursing care: position (supine, legs elevated if appropriate), oxygen, IV fluids as prescribed (crystalloids — Ringer's lactate, 0.9% saline), monitor response (heart rate, BP, urine output via catheter, mental state), and prepare vasopressors. Blood transfusion safety: confirm identity at the bedside (patient ID band, prescription and blood unit label — two checkers), baseline observations, observe closely especially in the first 15 minutes (acute haemolytic reactions — fever, rigors, back pain, hypotension, haemoglobinuria: stop the transfusion immediately, keep the line open with saline, notify the doctor and blood bank, return the unit), complete within 4 hours of removal from storage, and document. Other reactions: febrile non-haemolytic, allergic, TACO (circulatory overload) and TRALI.

topics.title: Perioperative Nursing
topics.summary: Preoperative preparation, intraoperative roles, safe surgery checklist and immediate postoperative care.

material.heading: Preoperative and intraoperative
material.body: Preoperative nursing: confirm identity, informed consent (obtained by the surgeon; nurse checks it is signed and understood), fasting (6 hours solids, 2 hours clear fluids), site marking, removal of jewellery, prostheses, make-up and nail polish (pulse oximetry), pre-medication, baseline observations, investigations (FBC, genotype, grouping and cross-matching, electrolytes), skin preparation (shower; clip, don't shave), antithrombotic stockings, and patient education (deep breathing, coughing, early mobilisation). Intraoperative roles: scrub nurse (sterile field, instruments, counts of swabs, sharps and instruments — at the start, before closing cavities, and at skin closure), circulating nurse (non-sterile, supplies, documentation), and anaesthetic nurse. The WHO Surgical Safety Checklist: Sign In (before induction — identity, site, procedure, consent, allergies, airway risk, blood loss risk), Time Out (before incision — team introductions, antibiotic prophylaxis within 60 minutes, anticipated critical events), Sign Out (before leaving theatre — counts correct, specimen labelling, equipment problems, recovery concerns). Positioning prevents pressure injuries and nerve damage; diathermy safety requires correct plate placement.
keyPoints: Sign In, Time Out, Sign Out

material.heading: Postoperative care
material.body: Post-anaesthesia care unit (recovery room): maintain airway (jaw thrust, oropharyngeal airway, recovery position), oxygen, monitor observations every 5–15 minutes, assess pain (and give prescribed analgesia), nausea and vomiting, wound and drains, fluid balance and temperature (prevent hypothermia); discharge from recovery using criteria (e.g. Aldrete score). Ward care: regular observations, pain management (multimodal), early mobilisation and deep breathing (prevent atelectasis, pneumonia and DVT), fluid balance and urinary output (retention is common), wound care (aseptic dressing; watch for infection on days 3–7), drain care, nutrition, and early warning of complications — haemorrhage (primary, reactionary within 24 hours, secondary after days — infection), shock, respiratory complications, DVT/PE, wound dehiscence (serosanguinous discharge — cover with sterile moist dressing, keep patient supine with knees flexed, call surgeon), anastomotic leak, and paralytic ileus. Discharge education on wound care, activity and warning signs.
keyPoints: Dehiscence: moist sterile dressing, knees flexed

topics.title: Special Critical Care Situations
topics.summary: Care of patients with head injury, burns, poisoning, renal failure and neonates in intensive care.

material.heading: Neurological, burns and poisoning
material.body: Head injury nursing: neurological observations (GCS, pupils, limb power, vital signs) every 15–60 minutes with escalation of a drop in GCS ≥ 2 or new pupil changes; head elevation 30° with neck in neutral, avoid tight tube ties around the neck, maintain oxygenation and normocapnia, control fever and glucose, seizure precautions, and prevent complications of immobility. Burns nursing: fluid resuscitation per Parkland with hourly urine output monitoring (0.5 mL/kg/h adults; 1 mL/kg/h children), airway observation (inhalation injury), pain relief, infection prevention (aseptic dressings, isolation), nutrition (high protein and calorie), positioning and splinting to prevent contractures, and psychological support. Poisoning: ABC, identify substance, decontamination as prescribed, antidotes (atropine for organophosphates, naloxone for opioids, N-acetylcysteine for paracetamol), monitor, and assess suicide risk with mental health referral.

material.heading: Renal and neonatal intensive care
material.body: Acute kidney injury nursing: strict fluid balance, daily weights, monitoring potassium (ECG changes — peaked T waves), restricting fluids/potassium as prescribed, care of dialysis access (AV fistula — no BP or cannulation in that arm; check thrill and bruit; central venous catheters — aseptic handling), and monitoring during haemodialysis (hypotension, cramps, disequilibrium). Neonatal intensive care nursing: thermoregulation (incubators, radiant warmers, kangaroo mother care), infection prevention (hand hygiene — the most important measure), respiratory support (bubble CPAP — a low-cost, effective intervention widely introduced in Nigerian newborn units), phototherapy care (eye shields, hydration, turning, monitoring bilirubin), feeding (expressed breast milk, nasogastric or cup feeding), glucose monitoring, and family involvement. Accurate drug calculation and double-checking are vital because of tiny doses.
